# Machine learning 

## Introduction

- Bayesian modeling and judgement prediction 

    - ideal for situations with **high uncertainty** and **little data**
    
    - evaluation of proposed solution complicated (not enough data)
    
    - uncertainty treatment is key
    
    - models are **specific** to purpose
    
- Machine learning

    - ideal for situations with **much data**
    
    - evaluation simple (use part of the data)
    
    - focus on **whatever works**
    
    - models are **general** (and scalable)
    
    - great sucess in text (language models) and vision

### Summary

- estimation

    - models
    
    - loss function / scoring rules
    
    - optimization

- in-sample vs out-of-sample

    - over-fitting, bias-variance tradeoff

    - train, validate/test

- Example: k-nearest neighbors

---

- deep learning

    - neural nets
    
    - stochastic gradient descend
    
    - best practices

- Example: prediction with neural net

- language models as next-token predictions
    


### Setting

- here we focus on the setting, where we want to 

    - predict some $y$ (normally a real or binary variable)
    
    - given information $x$ (normally a vector)
    
    - based on a sample of data $\mathcal D = \large((y_1,x_1),\dots, (y_n,x_n)\large)$
    
    - "supervised learning"
    
- we use generic models $m(x,\theta)$

    - use input $x$
    
    - have some parameters $\theta$
    
    - output a prediction for $y$ 
    
- Approach:

    - learn $\theta$ from data $\mathcal D \Rightarrow \hat \theta$
    
    - then predict $\hat p = m(x,\hat \theta)$
    
## Estimation

- Estimate $\hat \theta$ with some loss function $L(y,\hat y)$ (or scoring rule)
  $$\hat \theta = \arg\min_\theta \sum_i L(y_i,m(x_i, \theta))$$
  
    - for each $\theta$
    
    - compute **prediction** [$m(x_i,\theta)$]{.blue}

    - **loss** $L(y, \color{blue}{m(x_i,\theta)})$
    
    - **sum** over all observations $\sum_i L(\dots)$
    
    - **minimize** this expression with respect to $\theta$

- Also called **fitting** a parameter/model to the data

### OLS comparison

- the procedure above is general and includes the OLS regression if

    - model is linear $m(x,\theta)=x \theta$
    
    - loss is the squared error $L(y,\hat y)=(y-\hat y)^2$
    
- in this simple case, the minimization can be solved with "ordinary" analytics

- for more complex methods and different loss functions the minimization cannot be solved analytically

    - need to do this computationally

## In-sample versus out-of-sample

- It is common to use a training data set $\mathcal{D}$ for fitting a statistical model ($x_i$ is a $p$-dim. vector of predictors) 

- Training data are aka **in-sample** data

- We're interested in **out-of-sample** prediction of new data point

- A model that does well in-sample need not do well out-of-sample, and vice versa 


### OLS out-of-sample

- In particular, complex models tend to do well in-sample but not out-of-sample 

- you may know this from OLS with increasing number of covariates

    - if you have $n$ covariates (where none can be constructed by linear combination from the others) you can explain all the data
    
    - perfect in-sample fit
    
    - normally terrible out-of-sample prediction model


### Separate Training and Testing

- One solution to overfitting is **separating the data $D$** into     

    - **training set $D^T$** and 
    
    - **validation set $D^V$**
    
- training set

    - large proportion of data
    
    - used to fit the parameter
    
- test/validation set

    - can evaluate **out-of-sample** predictive accuracy

    - used to choose model, hyperparameters, or fitting procedure

### In-sample versus out-of-sample 

![Source: [@hastie2009elements]](plots/Fig2_11.png)

::: {style="text-align: right;"}
Source: Hastie et al. (2009)
:::

### In-sample versus out-of-sample prediction

- Fitting a complex model that does poorly out-of-sample is called `overfitting' 

    - See book by @silver2012signal for many good examples 

- Finding an appropriate level of model complexity is a key challenge of predictive modeling

    - simple model $\Rightarrow$ can't fully adjust $\Rightarrow$ bias in prediction
    
    - complex model $\Rightarrow$ less data per parameter $\Rightarrow$ higher (sampling) variance

- Next look at this for a specific (simple) model: $k$-nearest-neighbor (KNN) regression 


## Example: KNN regression

- Notation follows @hastie2009elements, Ch. 2.3 

- For a given $x$, KNN regression makes the prediction 
$$\hat y(x) = \frac{1}{k} \sum_{i \in N_k(x)} y_i,$$
where $N_k(x)$ denotes the $k$ nearest neighbors of $x$ in the training sample (in terms of Euclidian distance) 

- the parameter of this model is $k$

    - how many neighbours do I use?
    
    - more neighbours: more accurate, but neighbours less relevant
    
    - less neighbours: more noisy, but neighbours more relevant

### KNN simulation

- we look at a simple model with univariate real-valued $x$ and $$y \sim \mathcal N(x,\epsilon^2)$$

    - linear regression would have been a good model
    
    - KNN is more flexible


### k=1 and k=9


![Source: https://web.stanford.edu/class/stats202/notes/Linear-regression/K-nearest-neighbors.html](plots/knn.png){width="400" fig-align="center"}

### KNN regression with $k = 1$

- Use only one nearest neighbor (NN) for prediction

- Training sample:

    - Every observation is its own NN, so $\hat Y(x_i) = y_i,~i = 1, \ldots,N$

    - Hence, perfect fit (zero error) in training sample

- Likely poor test sample performance (predictions very variable due to overfitting)

### KNN regression with $k = 1$: Simulation example

```{r echo = FALSE}
set.seed(2020)
# Function for k nearest neighbor regression
KNN_prediction <- function(x, y, x0, K){
  
  # Nr of predictions
  n0 <- length(x0)
  
  # Vector to store predictions
  pred <- data.frame(x0 = x0, y0 = NA)
  
  # Loop through x0 values
  for (jj in 1:n0){
    # Squared deviations from x0[jj]
    aux <- (x - x0[jj])^2
    
    # Find nearest neighbors
    # First rank squared deviations
    rk <- rank(aux, ties.method = "random")
    
    # Find indexes of nearest neighbors
    ind_nn <- which(rk <= K)
    
    # Compute mean y value for neighbors
    pred$y0[jj] <- mean(y[ind_nn])
    
  }
  
  return(pred)
  
}

N <- 120
s <- 1.8
plot_l <- 5
c <- grey(.5, .8)
x <- rnorm(N)
y <- x + rnorm(N, sd = s)
x_test <- rnorm(N)
y_test <- x_test + rnorm(N, sd = s)
pred_test <- KNN_prediction(x, y, x_test, 1)
par(mfrow = c(2, 1))
plot(x = y, y = y, bty = "n", xlab = "Prediction", ylab = "Outcome", main = "Training sample (k = 1)", 
     pch = 20, ylim = c(-plot_l, plot_l), xlim = c(-plot_l, plot_l), col = c)
plot(x = pred_test$y0, y = y_test, bty = "n", xlab = "Prediction", ylab = "Outcome", 
     main = "Test sample (k = 1)", pch = 20, ylim = c(-plot_l, plot_l), 
     xlim = c(-plot_l, plot_l), col = c)
```


### KNN regression with $k = N$

- Use N nearest neighbors for prediction

- Training sample:

    - Every observation is among the N nearest neighbors of all other observations, so $\hat Y(x_i) = 1/N \sum_{i=1}^N y_i, i = 1, \ldots,N$

    - Hence, fairly high in-sample error

- Test sample performance likely to leave room for improvement (method does not exploit potential information in $x$)


### KNN regression with $k = N$: Simulation example

```{r echo = FALSE}
par(mfrow = c(2, 1))
plot(x = rep(mean(y), N), y = y, bty = "n", xlab = "Prediction", ylab = "Outcome", 
     main = "Training sample (k = N)", pch = 20, ylim = c(-plot_l, plot_l), 
     xlim = c(-plot_l, plot_l), col = c)
plot(x = rep(mean(y), N), y = y_test, bty = "n", xlab = "Prediction", ylab = "Outcome", 
     main = "Test sample (k = N)", pch = 20, ylim = c(-plot_l, plot_l), 
     xlim = c(-plot_l, plot_l), col = c)
```

### KNN example: Comments

- Example highlights that training sample performance and test sample performance are distinct

- Both above choices of $k$ are suboptimal: $k = 1$ overfits, $k = N$ underfits

- Need to find the right model complexity (represented by $k$) in order to attain good test sample performance. Need to avoid both over- and underfitting.

### Which $k$ does best in test/validation sample?

```{r echo = FALSE}
mse <- data.frame(k = 1:N, mse = NA)
for (kk in 1:N){
  mse$mse[kk] <- mean((y_test - KNN_prediction(x, y, x_test, kk)$y0)^2)
}
plot(1:N, mse$mse, bty = "n", xlab = "k", ylab = "Test sample mean squared error", col = c, pch = 20)
abline(v = mse$k[which.min(mse$mse)], lwd = 2)

```

### Simulation example: Plots for (ex post) optimal choice of $k$

```{r echo = FALSE}
k_opt <- which.min(mse$mse)
pred_train_new <- KNN_prediction(x, y, x, k_opt)
pred_test_new <- KNN_prediction(x, y, x_test, k_opt)
par(mfrow = c(2, 1))
plot(x = pred_train_new$y0, y, bty = "n", xlab = "Prediction", ylab = "Outcome", 
     main = paste0("Training sample (k = ", k_opt, ")"), pch = 20, ylim = c(-plot_l, plot_l), 
     xlim = c(-plot_l, plot_l), col = c)
plot(x = pred_test_new$y0, y_test, bty = "n", xlab = "Prediction", ylab = "Outcome", 
     main = paste0("Test sample (k = ", k_opt, ")"), pch = 20, ylim = c(-plot_l, plot_l), 
     xlim = c(-plot_l, plot_l), col = c)
```

# Neural Networks

## Introduction

- So far, you know

    - linear models $\hat y(x)=\sum_k x_k \theta_k$
    
    - KNN $\hat y(x) = \frac{1}{k} \sum_{i \in N_k(x)} y_i,$

- but what if model is

    - not linear and
    
    - we want to allow more complex interactions?

- **Neural Networks (NNs):** 

    - Inspired by biological neurons
    
    - flexible functions
    
    - form the basis of **Deep Learning**    

## Theory

### The Basic Unit: Neuron (Perceptron)

- A single neuron 

    - takes multiple **inputs** $x_i$, 
    
    - computes a **weighted sum**, adds a bias $+b$,
    $$z = (\sum_{i} w_i x_i)+b$$  
    
    - and applies a non-linear **activation function** $a = f(z)$

![Simplified Neuron Diagram. Source: https://upload.wikimedia.org](plots/nn.png){width=70%}



### Activation Functions: Adding Non-Linearity

- If we only used linear combinations ($z = wx+b$), the whole network would just be one big linear transformation. 

- Activation functions $f$ introduce non-linearity, allowing NNs to model complex relationships.

- **ReLU (Rectified Linear Unit):** $f(z) = \max(0, z)$. 
    
    - Efficient, widely used in hidden layers. 
    
- **Linear:** $f(z) = z$. 

    - used in the *output layer* for regression tasks


---

- **Logistic:** $f(z) = \frac {1} {1+e^{-z}}$
    
    - used in the output layer for binary probability prediction
    
- **Softmax:** $f(z_i) = \frac{e^{z_i}}{\sum_{j=1}^K e^{z_j}} \quad \text{for } i=1, \dots, K$
   
    - used in the output layer for finite outcome probability prediction ("classification")





### Building Layers: Neural Networks

- Neurons are organized into layers:
    
    - **Input Layer:** The raw data 
    
    - **Hidden Layer(s):** Can have multiple hidden layers ("Deep" Learning). This is where complex patterns are learned.
    
    - **Output Layer:** Produces the final prediction.
    
![Neural network with two hidden layers. Source: https://upload.wikimedia.org](plots/nn_full.png){width=70%}


### Identification and interpretation

- in econometrics, we normally focus on other aspects of models like identification and interpretation

- Machine learning/deep learning focuses more on predictive performance

- **identification**: Is there a unique parameter solving the optimization?

    - linear regression and OLS: Yes
    
    - neural networks: No, multiple!
    
- **interpretation** of parameters

    - linear regression: Yes.
    
    - neural networks: No. "Blackbox".



## Estimation

### The Goal: Learning Weights & Biases

- How does the network learn its parameters $\theta$

    - consists of weights ($w$) and biases ($b$)?

- **Define a Loss Function:** Measures how "wrong" the network's predictions ($\hat{y}$) are compared to the true values ($y$).

    - **Regression:** Mean Squared Error (MSE) is common: $L = \frac{1}{N} \sum (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2$

    - **Classification:** log score ("cross-entropy") is common.

- **Goal:** Find the weights and biases that *minimize* the loss function across the training data.


### Estimation

- Bayesian estimation possible?

    - in theory yes, works for small models, and little data
    
    - otherwise convergence problems
    
    - no sensible priors on weights and biases
    
- Instead: optimize loss function on training data

    - First approach: Gradient descend

### Gradient descend

- **Intuition:** Imagine the loss function as a landscape with hills and valleys. We want to find the lowest point (minimum loss).

- **Gradient:** The gradient ($\nabla L$) points in the direction of the *steepest ascent* of the loss function.

- **Gradient Descent Algorithm:**

    1. Initialize weights/biases randomly.
    
    2. Calculate the gradient of the loss function with respect to each weight/bias. 
    
    3. Update each weight/bias by taking a small step in the *opposite* direction of its gradient:
    
       $w_{new} = w_{old} - \eta \frac{\partial L}{\partial w_{old}}$
       ($\eta$ is the *learning rate* - controls step size).
    
    4. Repeat steps 2-3 until the loss converges.


### Stochastic gradient descend

- Calculating the gradient using the *entire* training dataset is computationally expensive for large datasets

- **Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD):** Updates weights using the gradient calculated from a random subset of data for each update

    - Noisy, but much faster, updates
    
    - Can escape shallow local minima
    
    - subset is called "batch"
    
    - loop through all data multiple times (called "epoch")
    
- Variants like **Adam** [@kingma2014adam] adapt the learning rate during training and often converge faster


### Uncertainty quantification

- NN can be used with probability distribution as output

    - probabilistic prediction
    
    - unfortunately often uncalibrated
    
- NN can be used with point predictions as output

    - point prediction
    
    - uncertainty quantification difficult
    
- There exist several approaches:
    
    - Ensemble: estimate multiple models and their predictions
    
    - Monte-carlo dropout: randomly deactivate neurons and compute predictions

## Practice

### Overfitting

- NNs are very flexible and can learn complex patterns.
- **Overfitting:** The network learns the *training data* too well, including its noise and specific quirks. It performs poorly on new, unseen data (poor generalization).
- **Signs:** Training loss keeps decreasing, but validation/test loss starts increasing.

![Overfitting Diagram, source:https://upload.wikimedia.org](plots/Overfitted_Data.png){width=60%}

### Regularization

- **Need Regularization:** Techniques to prevent overfitting.

- Standard regularization uses adapted loss functions that **penalize** extreme weights, e.g.
    $$L(y,\hat y, w) = (y-\hat y)^2 \color{red}{+ \lambda \sum_k |w_k|}$$
    - $\lambda$ governs importance of penalty
    
    - doing this in OLS regression recovers **Lasso** estimation

### Dropout

- **Dropout** is a simpler and often more effective regularization technique.

    - **Mechanism:** During training, randomly "drop out" a fraction of neurons

    - A different set of neurons is dropped each time.
    
    - **Intuition:** Forces the network to learn more robust representations.


### Transfer learning

- **Problem:** Training large neural networks requires massive datasets
    
    - What if our specific task has limited data?
    
- **Solution: Transfer Learning:** 

    - Take a **pre-trained model** (e.g., trained on related data)
    
    - update/fine-tune/extend it with your own training data
      
    - Feature Extraction: fix lower layers of pre-trained model and learn new layers on top
      
    - Fine-Tuning: Initialize your model with the pre-trained weights. Continue training on own data with much smaller training rate
      
- **Benefits:** Faster, cheaper, often better performance

- **Common Domains:** Image recognition, text, time series forecasting.




# Examples

## Software

- we will use **keras**

- keras is **build on top** of **pytorch** and **tensorflow**

- pytorch and tensorflow are the most used frameworks for deep learning

- keras allows simpler but less versatile control

- keras can be used in R and python directly

    

## Example with keras: real target, one covariate

- let's start with a simple mean prediction example

- we have a non-linear relationship of $y = sin(2x) + \epsilon$

    - $x \sim \mathcal N (0,1)$

- we want to predict $y$ for every $x$ based on a sample of 200 observations using 

    - neural networks
    
    - sample splitting to check results

### Code

```{r}
# Install necessary packages if you haven't already
# install.packages("keras")
# install.packages("tensorflow")
# tensorflow::install_tensorflow() # Run this once to install TensorFlow backend for Keras in R
# keras::install_keras() # Run this once to install backend for Keras in R

# Load necessary libraries
library(keras)
library(tensorflow)
library(ggplot2) # For plotting
library(dplyr) # For data manipulation

# Set random seed for reproducibility
set.seed(42)
tf$random$set_seed(42)

# 1. Generate simulated data
n_samples <- 200
# x standard normal
x <- rnorm(n_samples, mean = 0, sd = 1)
# save as matrix
x <- matrix(x, ncol = 1)
# Generate y values based on sin(x) with added random noise
y <- sin(2*x) + rnorm(n_samples, mean = 0, sd = .1)
y <- matrix(y, ncol = 1) # Ensure y is a matrix for Keras


# 3. Define a neural network, 
# specify input (1-dimensional here)
model <- keras_model_sequential(input_shape = c(1))  |> 
  # first hidden layer: 64 neurons, ReLU activation
  layer_dense(units = 64, activation = 'relu' ) |>
  # Second hidden layer: 64 neurons, ReLU activation
  layer_dense(units = 64, activation = 'relu') |>
  # Output layer: 1 neuron, no activation (linear) for regression output
  layer_dense(units = 1, activation = "linear")

# 4. Compile the model
# Use the Adam optimizer
# Use Mean Squared Error as the loss function (common for regression)
model |> compile(
  optimizer = 'adam',
  loss = 'mse'
)

# 5. Train the model
# Train for 100 epochs
# Use a batch size of 32
# Use 20% of the training data for validation during training
# verbose = 0 means no training progress output per epoch
history <- model |> fit(
  x, y,
  epochs = 100,
  batch_size = 32,
  validation_split = 0.2,
  verbose = 0
)


# 7. Make predictions using the trained model on the sorted x data

# generate predictions from model
y_pred <- model |> predict(x)

# Create a data frame for easier handling
data_df <- data.frame(x = x[,1], y = y[,1], y_pred = y_pred)

# 8. Visualize the results using ggplot2
prediction_plot <- ggplot() +
  # scatter plot of data points
  geom_point(data = data_df, aes(x = x, y = y), alpha = 0.6, size = 1, color = "blue") +
  # line for predicted points
  geom_line(data = data_df |> arrange(x), 
            aes(x = x, y = y_pred), color = "red", size = 1)

```


### Results: loss

```{r}
plot(history)
```
### Results: predictions

```{r}
prediction_plot
```

## Example with keras (python)

- for a python solution check out the following [[colab]{.blue}](https://colab.research.google.com/drive/1S8FEMWn1z8G5SkY-AMzxB5FsVGBLbDi8?usp=sharing)

- or use the code below


### Python code

```python
import numpy as np
import tensorflow as tf
from tensorflow import keras
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# 1. Generate simulated data
np.random.seed(42) # for reproducibility
n_samples = 1000
x = np.random.normal(loc=0, scale=1, size=(n_samples, 1)) # x ~ N(0, 1)
y = np.sin(x) + np.random.normal(loc=0, scale=0.1, size=(n_samples, 1)) # y = sin(x) + some noise

# Sort x for plotting purposes later
sorted_indices = np.argsort(x.flatten())
x_sorted = x[sorted_indices]
y_sorted = y[sorted_indices]

# 2. Split the data
x_train, x_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(x, y, test_size=0.2, random_state=42)

# 3. Define a simple Keras model
model = keras.Sequential([
    keras.layers.Dense(64, activation='relu', input_shape=(1,)), # Input layer and a hidden layer with ReLU activation
    keras.layers.Dense(64, activation='relu'), # Another hidden layer
    keras.layers.Dense(1) # Output layer with no activation for regression
])

# 4. Compile the model
model.compile(optimizer='adam', # Adam optimizer is a good default
              loss='mse') # Mean Squared Error is suitable for regression

# 5. Train the model
history = model.fit(x_train, y_train,
                    epochs=100, # Number of training epochs
                    batch_size=32, # Number of samples per gradient update
                    validation_split=0.2, # Use a portion of training data for validation
                    verbose=0) # Don't show training progress for each epoch

# 6. Evaluate the model
loss = model.evaluate(x_test, y_test, verbose=0)
print(f"Mean Squared Error on test data: {loss:.4f}")

# 7. Make predictions
y_pred = model.predict(x_sorted)

# 8. Visualize the results
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))
plt.scatter(x, y, label='Simulated Data', alpha=0.6, s=10)
plt.plot(x_sorted, y_pred, color='red', linewidth=2, label='Keras Model Predictions')
plt.title('Keras Model Prediction of y = sin(x)')
plt.xlabel('x')
plt.ylabel('y')
plt.legend()
plt.grid(True)
plt.show()
```


## Example with keras: binary target

- next we consider a binary prediction target $y \sim Bernoulli(p(x))$ where $p(x)$ depends non-linearly on a 2-dimensional $x$

For $y=0$ we simulate $x$ values on a sinus curve
  
  - $x_1 \sim \mathcal N(0,1)$
  
  - $x_2 \sim \mathcal N(sin(x_1), 0.2^2)$
  
For $y=1$ we simulate covariates with

  - $x_1 \sim \mathcal N(0,1)$
  
  - $x_2 \sim \mathcal N(0,1)$
  
### Code: Data

```{r}
# Set random seed for reproducibility
set.seed(42)
tf$random$set_seed(42)

# 1. Generate simulated data
n_samples <- 1000
# x standard normal
x1 <- rnorm(n_samples, mean = 0, sd = 1)
# x2 standard normal
x2 <- rnorm(n_samples, mean = 0, sd = 1)
# half to noisy sinus curve
x2[(n_samples/2):n_samples] <-
  sin(x1[(n_samples/2):n_samples])+rnorm(n_samples/2,mean=0, sd=.2)
y <- c(rep(TRUE, n_samples/2), 
       rep(FALSE, n_samples/2))

```

---

```{r}
ggplot()+
  geom_point(data = data.frame(x=x1,y=x2,col=y), aes(x=x,y=y,col=col))
```


### Code 

```{r}
# reformat as matrix
y <- as.matrix(y)
x <- cbind(x1,x2)


# 3. Define a neural network, 
model <- keras_model_sequential(input_shape = c(2))  |> 
  layer_dense(units = 64, activation = 'relu', ) |>
  layer_dense(units = 64, activation = 'relu') |>
  # Output layer: 1 neuron, activation logistic ("sigmoid") for binary output
  layer_dense(units = 1, activation = "sigmoid")

# 4. Compile the model
# Use the Adam optimizer
# Use crossentropy as loss function equivalent to log score
# (common for classification/event prediction)
model |> compile(
  optimizer = 'adam',
  loss = "binary_crossentropy" 
)

# 5. Train the model
# Train for 100 epochs
# Use a batch size of 32
# Use 20% of the training data for validation during training
# verbose = 0 means no training progress output per epoch
history <- model |> fit(
  x, y,
  epochs = 100,
  batch_size = 32,
  validation_split = 0.2,
  verbose = 0
)


# 7. Make predictions using the trained model on the sorted x data

# generate predictions from model
y_pred <- model |> predict(x)

# Create a data frame for easier handling
data_df <- data.frame(x1 = x[,1],x2=x[,2], y = y_pred)

# 8. Visualize the results using ggplot2
prediction_plot <- ggplot() +
  # scatter plot of data points
  geom_point(data = data_df, aes(x = x1, y =x2,col=y))
```
### Results

```{r}
prediction_plot

```

### Summary: Examples

- neural networks can be fit with keras

- if they work, they often do so very well

    - sometimes hard to find a working specification

- examples were with 1 or 2 dimensional covariate / input feature $x$ for illustration

    - neural networks mostly used in higher dimensions

## Summary: Neural networks

- general and flexible class of models

- good solution for rich data environments

    - transfer learning if data is scarce but adjecent data is available
    
- difficult to do uncertainty quantification

- difficult to interpret model parameters


### Pitfall: Off support predictions

```{r, echo=F, out.width=300}

set.seed(12321)
x <- runif(10,-1,1)
y <- .4*x+rnorm(10,0,.1)

ggplot(data.frame(x,y),aes(x,y))+
  geom_point()+
  xlim(c(-1,3))+geom_vline(xintercept = 2)+
  geom_smooth(method = lm, formula = y ~ splines::ns(x,df=2), se = FALSE)+
  theme(text = element_text(size=16))

```

- we call the observed $x$ values, the **support** of our data

    - here support is $[-1,1]$
    
- off-support predictions rely on addition assumptions

    - predict for $x=2$?!

### Other methods

- Deep learning (Machine Learning with neural networks with many layers) had the most success recently

- for standard prediction tasks (e.g, the winning approaches in kaggle competitions) other methods may be more adequate

    - penalized regression (e.g., lasso)
    
    - random forests
    
    - support vector machines
    
    - gaussian processes
    
    - many others
